author: Alexander, J.

reason: The abstract says the essay criticizes 'the historical and philosophical attitudes to political thought found in the writings of John Dunn and Michael Oakeshott'. author: Annan, N.
citation: Our Age: Portrait of a Generation (London: Weidenfeld and Nicolson, 1990).
reason: Our Age has a chapter titled 'The Deviants - Michael Oakeshott' (Part III, alongside chapters on other 'deviants' such as Evelyn Waugh). It opens: 'On one count he was of his times and no deviant.' Annan is critical (e.g. 'Oakeshott was exercising his negative capability at rather a cheap rate') and quotes 'an unforgettable passage' of Oakeshott. Annan also says it was Hayek and Friedman, 'rather than Oakeshott', who inspired the new conservatism.

author: Arditi, B.
citation: ‘Populism as a Spectre of Democracy: A Response to Canovan’, Political Studies, 52 (2004), pp. 135-43.
reason: Arditi examines at length Canovan's reworking of Oakeshott's distinction between the politics of faith and the politics of scepticism. He quotes and cites The Politics of Faith and the Politics of Scepticism (Fuller ed.) many times. He discusses Oakeshott's idea of the 'trimmer' and the middle region of movement, his description of the two styles as a 'concordia discors', and his claim about the ambiguity of political vocabulary. He then argues that, if the gap between the two styles is structural to modern politics, it explains political radicalism generally and not populism specifically.

author: Bain, W.
citation: ‘Are There Any Lessons of History? The English School and the Activity of Being an Historian’, International Politics, 44 (2007), pp. 513-30.
reason: According to the abstract, Bain finds that Bull and Butterfield cannot fully support the English School's claim that historical knowledge matters for international relations. He turns to Oakeshott's view of history as a kind of fable to fill that gap. He concludes that English School theorists keep a role for history by denying it any didactic or practical function. The title echoes Oakeshott's essay 'The Activity of Being an Historian'.

author: Barber, B.
citation: The Conquest of Politics: Liberal Philosophy in Democratic Times (Princeton: Princeton University Press, 1988).
reason: Chapter 6, 'Conserving Politics: Michael Oakeshott and the Conversation of Political Theory' (beginning p. 152; running heads 'Michael Oakeshott' to at least p. 174), is devoted to Oakeshott. Barber criticizes Oakeshott for seeking to insulate the pure theorist from practice, and turns Oakeshott's own insistence on the primacy of practice and conversation against him. He revises his earlier article 'Conserving Politics: The Political Theory of Michael Oakeshott', Government and Opposition.

author: Boucher, D.
citation: and Andrew Vincent, British Idealism and Political Theory (Edinburgh: Edinburgh University Press, 2000).
reason: Chapter 7, 'Michael Oakeshott: The Non-Economic Character of Civil Association', is devoted to Oakeshott. It covers his philosophy, with a section 'Oakeshott and Philosophy' on Experience and Its Modes and the modes; the conversation of mankind and The Voice of Poetry; On Human Conduct; and civil association.

author: Canovan, M.
citation: ‘Trust the People: Populism and Two Faces of Democracy’, Political Studies, 47 (1999), pp. 2-16.
reason: The abstract says the paper adapts Michael Oakeshott's distinction between 'the politics of faith' and 'the politics of scepticism' (from The Politics of Faith and the Politics of Scepticism). From it the paper builds its analysis of democracy as having two opposing faces, 'pragmatic' and 'redemptive'. It argues that the tension between them makes populism a perennial possibility. Oakeshott's distinction is therefore the framework of the whole argument.

author: Coats, W.J., Jr.
citation: Political Theory and Practice: Eight Essays on a Theme (Selinsgrove : Susquehanna University Press, 2003).
reason: Two of the eight essays concern Oakeshott: ch. 3 'Oakeshott's Descartes, Vico's Descartes' and ch. 7 'Michael Oakeshott and the Poetic Character of Human Activity'. Google Books lists 'Michael Oakeshott' and 'Oakeshott's critique' among the book's common terms. Another source describes one essay as comparing Oakeshott and Leo Strauss on the Romans and Roman law, and another as a reply to John Liddington's analysis (of Oakeshott).

author: Collingwood, R.G.
citation: The Idea of History (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1946).
reason: In Part IV (the section on English philosophy of history after Bury) Collingwood gives a multi-page account of Oakeshott's Experience and its Modes: history as a 'mode' of experience, an arrest of experience at a certain point. He praises it as a 'brilliant and penetrating account' that vindicates the autonomy of historical thought, then criticizes Oakeshott for failing to explain why history arises as a necessary mode of experience. He also argues there is a way between the horns of Oakeshott's past/present dilemma. Index: Oakeshott, M.B., 151-9 (also 180, 289).

author: Dallmayr, F.
citation: ‘Conversation Across Boundaries: Political Theory and Global Diversity’, Millennium: Journal for International Studies, 30 (2001), pp. 331-47.
reason: The abstract says the essay starts from Oakeshott's 'The Voice of Poetry in the Conversation of Mankind' and his defence of a mode of discourse not subservient to science or technical utility. author: Dray, W.H.

author: Dray, W.H.

He sets out Oakeshott's view that the historian is concerned with the individual, that explaining events by general laws would mean 'the complete destruction of history', and that 'the method of the historian is never' to explain by generalization. Index: Oakeshott, Michael, 7-10, 13, 15, 37.

Part three uses that distinction to analyse the moral and political constitution of the UK National Health Service. Oakeshott's distinction is the paper's central analytic tool.

author: Germino, D.

author: Gilmour, I.

author: Gray, J.

It draws on Rationalism in Politics, On Human Conduct, and Experience and Its Modes, describing the latter as a work 'which Oakeshott was never able to improve, and whose central claims he never retracted'. The essay first appeared in Common Knowledge.

author: Jackson, R.
citation: The Global Covenant: Human Conduct in a World of States (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2000).
reason: Jackson builds on the 'political theory of human conduct' presented in Oakeshott's Rationalism in Politics and On Human Conduct, alongside Collingwood. The book's subtitle echoes this. He discusses Oakeshott's 'civil association', based on non-instrumental relations, and notes that Oakeshott denies that civil association exists in international relations. He also cites Hobbes on Civil Association and quotes Oakeshott on politics and conversation.

author: Meiland, J.W.
citation: Scepticism and Historical Knowledge (New York: Random House, 1965).
reason: Chapter 2 is titled 'Oakeshott: Is History Concerned with Past Events?' (beginning p. 41). It includes a section 'Oakeshott and Historical Scepticism' on Oakeshott's Experience and its Modes, covering the postulates of history, his denial that history yields practical wisdom, and his view that history is not concerned with the past. Chapter 3, 'Collingwood: Can the Past Be Present?', opens with 'Collingwood and Oakeshott' and argues that Collingwood does not succeed in refuting Oakeshott. Index: v, 7, 8, 28, 41ff, 63-64, 193-4.

author: Minogue, K.R.

author: Minogue, K.R.
citation: ‘Parts and Wholes: Twentieth Century Interpretation of Thomas Hobbes’, Annales de la Catedra Francisco Suarez, 14 (1974), pp. 77-108.

It calls his reading 'more elevated and more romantic' than earlier ones and sets out Oakeshott's three traditions of political philosophy (Reason and Nature, Will and Artifice, Rational Will), with Leviathan as the masterpiece of Will and Artifice. It also contrasts Oakeshott's treatment of Hobbes's moral theory with Leslie Stephen's psychological egoism, and returns to Oakeshott around pp. 105-6.

author: Mouffe, C.

In a section titled 'The Political Community: Universitas or Societas?' she says Oakeshott's On Human Conduct 'can be very illuminating'. She takes up his societas/universitas distinction and his idea of the respublica to find 'an alternative to the limitations of liberalism'. She also cites Hobbes on Civil Association, and criticizes Oakeshott because 'what is completely missing in Oakeshott is division and antagonism'.

author: Nardin, T.

He uses Oakeshott's distinction between relationship in terms of common purposes and relationship in terms of rules (civil association) as the frame for international society. He also refers to Oakeshott's 'extended discussion of the idea of the modern' state.

author: Nyiri, J.C.
